facts.statement: The package exports getLastCsrfToken with no input and setLastCsrfToken with a string token input to read and write the stored CSRF token state.
The package public barrel exports CSRF_HEADER_NAME, fetchWithCsrf, extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders, setLastCsrfToken, and getLastCsrfToken from ./csrf/csrf.
addCsrfToRequestHeaders accepts an optional HeadersInit and returns a new header container that adds or overwrites x-csrf-token with the current stored token value.
extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders accepts an optional Headers object and reads x-csrf-token from it when available.
fetchWithCsrf accepts an optional RequestInit options object; when present, its fields are shallow-merged into default GET options before headers are reassigned.
fetchWithCsrf accepts resource as RequestInfo or URL and returns the Response from fetch after post-response token extraction.
The CSRF header name is a fixed exported constant x-csrf-token and is not configurable through function parameters.
fetchWithCsrf starts from GET defaults derived from BASE_REQUEST, so the default method is GET with redirect follow, mode cors, and credentials include.

After option merging, fetchWithCsrf always replaces mergedOptions.headers with the result of addCsrfToRequestHeaders, ensuring x-csrf-token is present from stored state even if headers were supplied by the caller.
Caller-supplied RequestInit fields override the default GET options during object spread before headers are reassigned.
Inspected test source models a call path where a caller-provided mode value no-cors is preserved by the same shallow merge pattern used by fetchWithCsrfMock.
Module state starts with lastCsrfToken initialized to the empty string, and getLastCsrfToken returns the current stored value.
extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders leaves stored token state unchanged when the header object is absent, the x-csrf-token header is missing, or the header value is an empty string.
extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders updates stored token state only when responseHeaders.get('x-csrf-token') yields a nonempty string.
fetchWithCsrf sends the currently stored token in the request headers before fetch, then may update the stored token from the response headers before returning the Response.
setLastCsrfToken unconditionally assigns the provided string to the module-level lastCsrfToken state.

For browser cross-origin use, this source path conditionally depends on the destination allowing credentialed sharing, permitting the x-csrf-token request header, and exposing the x-csrf-token response header to script; repository source does not establish any server configuration for those conditions.
fetchWithCsrf adds the stored CSRF token to the outgoing request under the x-csrf-token header and then attempts to read x-csrf-token from the received response headers.

fetchWithCsrf issues its request to the caller-provided resource via fetch using credentials include by default, so request credentials are sent according to fetch's credential handling for that destination unless the caller overrides credentials.
If fetch rejects, fetchWithCsrf has no local catch or fallback in the source span, so the rejection would propagate to the caller.

fetchWithCsrf contains no branch that retries a request after a failed or non-2xx response; it performs one fetch call per invocation.

The package barrel exports fetchWithCsrf for consumers, and fetchWithCsrf accepts a resource argument typed as RequestInfo | URL plus an optional RequestInit options object.

When request headers are supplied, fetchWithCsrf passes mergedOptions.headers to addCsrfToRequestHeaders, which creates a new object by spreading the provided headers and then assigning the x-csrf-token property.

Caller-supplied RequestInit properties override the default options during object spread before headers are reassigned, and the test source exercises a custom mode value of no-cors in its local mock path.
If options are omitted, fetchWithCsrf starts from initGetRequest, so the request defaults to method GET with redirect follow, mode cors, and credentials include.

Regardless of any caller-provided headers object, fetchWithCsrf replaces mergedOptions.headers with the result of addCsrfToRequestHeaders, which writes x-csrf-token using the current stored token after spreading the supplied headers.
If the response x-csrf-token header is missing or empty, extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders leaves the previously stored token unchanged.
The module stores CSRF state in a module-level lastCsrfToken string initialized to an empty string, readable through getLastCsrfToken and writable through setLastCsrfToken.

fetchWithCsrf updates stored CSRF state only when the response x-csrf-token header value exists, is a string, and is nonempty, because extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders calls setLastCsrfToken only under that condition.

Before calling fetch, fetchWithCsrf adds an x-csrf-token request header whose value comes from module-held state, and after the response it reads x-csrf-token from response headers to update that state.
By default, fetchWithCsrf sends requests with credentials include and mode cors, then calls the global fetch with the caller-supplied resource and merged options.

For browser cross-origin use, because fetchWithCsrf defaults to credentials include and mode cors, successful requests conditionally depend on the response permitting the requesting origin and credentialed sharing.

For browser cross-origin use, because fetchWithCsrf sends the non-safelisted x-csrf-token request header, successful requests conditionally depend on preflight permitting that request header and method.

For browser cross-origin use, because fetchWithCsrf reads x-csrf-token from response.headers in script, successful CSRF extraction conditionally depends on the response exposing the x-csrf-token header to script.
When fetch resolves, fetchWithCsrf returns the Response object it received after attempting CSRF extraction from response.headers.
fetchWithCsrf defines no retry, backoff, or recovery path; if fetch rejects, the function has no catch block and the rejection path is left to the underlying fetch call.
fetchWithCsrf does not inspect or branch on HTTP status before returning, so source establishes no built-in status-specific handling for non-2xx responses.

fetchWithCsrf always inspects response.headers after fetch resolves and may update the stored token through extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders before returning the same response object.
If the response exposes an 'x-csrf-token' header through Response.headers.get, fetchWithCsrf reads that response header and uses it to update local token state.
fetchWithCsrf adds the current stored token under the 'x-csrf-token' request header before calling fetch, so that token value is sent to the request destination.
fetchWithCsrf sends the request to the caller-provided resource using fetch with credentials:'include' unless the caller overrides that option.
If fetch rejects, fetchWithCsrf has no local catch block to transform the failure before return.
When fetch resolves, fetchWithCsrf returns the resulting Response object after attempting CSRF extraction and does not branch on HTTP status.
fetchWithCsrf contains no retry loop, fallback request, or status-specific recovery; it performs exactly one fetch call per invocation.

Consumers install a package whose declared entry points are built dist artifacts (main './dist/index.umd.cjs', module './dist/index.js', types './dist/index.d.ts') and whose published files list contains only 'dist'.
Using the CSRF helpers requires runtime availability of fetch Response and Headers interfaces because the implementation calls fetch(...) and responseHeaders?.get(...).
The package's public barrel exports exactly five CSRF-related symbols: CSRF_HEADER_NAME, fetchWithCsrf, extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders, setLastCsrfToken, and getLastCsrfToken.
addCsrfToRequestHeaders accepts an optional HeadersInit input and returns a new header object shape produced with object spread plus an x-csrf-token property.
extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders accepts an optional Headers object and reads the x-csrf-token response header from it.
fetchWithCsrf accepts resource as RequestInfo or URL and an optional RequestInit options object, then passes both to fetch after merging options and setting headers.
setLastCsrfToken accepts a string token value and getLastCsrfToken returns the stored token string.
After merging options, fetchWithCsrf always replaces mergedOptions.headers with the result of addCsrfToRequestHeaders on the current headers value before calling fetch.

Both initGetRequest and initPostRequest start from BASE_REQUEST, so their declared defaults include redirect:"follow", mode:"cors", and credentials:"include", with method set to GET or POST respectively.
When addCsrfToRequestHeaders runs, any existing x-csrf-token header value in the supplied headers is overwritten by the current stored token value.
fetchWithCsrf starts from initGetRequest defaults and then shallow-merges caller-supplied options over them, so caller options override the default RequestInit fields before headers are reassigned.
The module keeps CSRF state in a module-scoped lastCsrfToken string initialized to an empty string; getLastCsrfToken reads it and setLastCsrfToken assigns a new string value.
extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders updates stored state only when responseHeaders.get("x-csrf-token") returns a nonempty string.
fetchWithCsrf may mutate the stored token after a fetch by passing response.headers to extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders, and otherwise leaves token state unchanged when no nonempty header is present.

For browser cross-origin use, this operation conditionally depends on external response and preflight behavior that permits credentialed sharing, allows the request header, and exposes the response header if script must read it.
fetchWithCsrf reads the x-csrf-token header from the received Response headers and may store that response-supplied value for later requests.
fetchWithCsrf sends requests through the global fetch API with credentials:"include" and a request header named x-csrf-token containing the currently stored token value.
A resolved response of any HTTP status still flows through extractCsrfFromResponseHeaders before being returned, so token storage is not limited in source to success statuses.
When fetch resolves, fetchWithCsrf returns the same Response object it received after attempting CSRF header extraction.
fetchWithCsrf defines no local catch, status check, or retry loop around fetch, so any fetch rejection propagates from the awaited fetch call and no retry is attempted in this wrapper.
Consumers must configure the @dl npm scope to use the GitLab package registry and supply an auth token in npm configuration to install the package from the documented registry.
Runtime use of fetchWithCsrf requires a JavaScript environment that provides global fetch, Response headers access, and the Headers interface expected by the code path.
